topics.subject: Technical Standards

fib_noBlank.sentence: The effect that arises when two or more waves overlap in the same region so that the resultant disturbance at each point is the superposition of the individual waves.

The principle that, in a linear medium, the net displacement at any point and instant produced by several overlapping waves equals the algebraic sum of the displacements each wave would produce alone.

fib_noBlank.term: Energy transfer without bulk transport of matter
fib_noBlank.sentence: This phrase captures the defining physical characteristic of wave motion, including sound: a wave carries energy and momentum through a medium while the medium's particles only oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions and are not permanently displaced.

The resonance that occurs when air in a cavity vibrates like a mass on a spring: air in a narrow neck or opening acts as the mass, while the springiness of the enclosed air volume provides the restoring force, producing a single strong low-frequency resonance.
The degree to which two or more sound waves or signals hold a stable phase relationship over time.

The characteristic (specific acoustic) impedance of a medium is the product of its density and sound speed, z0 = rho*c, equal to the ratio of acoustic pressure to particle velocity for a plane progressive wave.
The homogeneous acoustic wave equation is the source-free linear partial differential equation that governs small-amplitude sound pressure in a lossless, uniform fluid.
The inhomogeneous acoustic wave equation is the wave equation with a non-zero right-hand side representing acoustic sources within the region.
Normal-incidence specific acoustic impedance is the complex ratio of sound pressure to normal particle velocity at a surface when a plane wave arrives perpendicularly.
The radiation (Sommerfeld) boundary condition is the physical requirement that, far from a source, acoustic energy only travels outward and no waves arrive from infinity.
Root-mean-square (RMS) sound pressure is the square root of the time-averaged square of the instantaneous sound pressure over a stated interval.
In linear acoustics the scalar (velocity) potential is a single scalar function whose spatial gradient gives the particle velocity and whose time derivative gives the sound pressure.
Surface (acoustic) impedance is the complex ratio of the sound pressure at a boundary to the resulting normal component of particle velocity into that boundary.

fib_noBlank.term: Why low frequencies have long wavelengths
fib_noBlank.sentence: This principle follows from the relation wavelength = sound speed / frequency: because the speed of sound is essentially fixed in a given medium, wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.

In acoustics, compression is the region of a longitudinal sound wave where the medium's particles are pushed together, producing a momentary increase in local pressure and density above the ambient value.
Principle that overlapping waves sum point-by-point, producing constructive and destructive interference.

A cylindrical wave is a sound field whose wavefronts form coaxial cylinders expanding from a line source, so the energy spreads over a surface that grows in proportion to distance rather than distance squared.

fib_noBlank.term: Sound as mechanical energy rather than an object
fib_noBlank.sentence: This concept frames sound as a transfer of mechanical energy through an elastic medium, not as a substance or object that moves from source to listener.

fib_noBlank.term: Sound propagation in gases, liquids, and solids
fib_noBlank.sentence: This term concerns how acoustic waves travel through different states of matter, where the speed and mode of propagation depend on the medium's elastic and inertial properties.
This principle states that sound, as a mechanical wave, requires a material medium — gas, liquid, or solid — to propagate, because it consists of oscillations of the medium's own particles.
A spherical wave is an acoustic wave that radiates outward from a compact, point-like source so that surfaces of constant phase are concentric spheres expanding at the speed of sound.

fib_noBlank.term: Transverse-wave diagrams used to represent longitudinal sound
fib_noBlank.sentence: This refers to the common convention of drawing sound, which is physically a longitudinal wave, as a transverse sinusoid in which a quantity such as pressure or displacement is plotted on a vertical axis against distance or time.

A phenomenon in which a vibrating body causes a nearby body to vibrate without direct contact, at the same or a harmonically related frequency, because energy transfers through the air or a shared structure when the second body's natural frequency matches a frequency present in the source.
Motion that repeats itself at regular, predictable intervals; the time for one full cycle is the period, and its inverse is the frequency.
The speed at which sound waves propagate through a medium; in air the commonly cited value is about 331 m/s (about 1087 ft/s) at 0 degrees C, rising to roughly 343 m/s at 20 degrees C.

A traveling (progressive) wave is a disturbance that propagates through a medium at a constant speed, carrying energy from one place to another while the medium's particles only oscillate about their rest positions with no net transport of matter.
The rate of change of the phase of a sinusoidal oscillation, equal to 2 pi times the ordinary frequency (omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi / T), expressed in radians per second.
Converts an angle from radians to degrees by multiplying by 180/π, the inverse of the degrees-to-radians factor.
Computes the period, the time in seconds for one complete cycle of a periodic signal, as the reciprocal of frequency.
Computes the time delay that produces a 180-degree (half-cycle) phase shift at a given frequency, equal to half the period.
Computes the time delay that produces a 90-degree (quarter-cycle) phase shift at a given frequency, equal to one quarter of the period.
Computes how many audio samples correspond to a given delay time at a specified sample rate.
Computes the delay time in seconds represented by a given number of audio samples at a specified sample rate.
Computes the distance sound travels in air during the time span of one audio sample, by dividing the speed of sound by the sample rate.
It is the standard measure of actual acoustic loudness in the physical world.
A logarithmic unit that expresses sound level, electrical signal amplitude, or frequency response magnitude.
The reference pressure of 20 micropascals (20 µPa) is the internationally standardized baseline against which sound pressure level in air is calculated, defined as 0 dB SPL.
A logarithmic measurement of acoustic pressure relative to a reference standard (20 micropascals), expressed in decibels, indicating the actual physical loudness of sound in a space.

fib_noBlank.term: Sound Intensity from RMS Pressure for a Plane Progressive Wave
fib_noBlank.sentence: For a plane progressive (free-field, far-field) sound wave, this gives the time-averaged acoustic intensity from the RMS sound pressure, because pressure and particle velocity are in phase and related by the characteristic impedance rho*c.
This is the inverse of the plane-wave intensity relation: given the intensity of a plane progressive wave, it returns the RMS sound pressure.

fib_secondary.term: Energy transfer without bulk transport of matter
fib_secondary.sentence: This phrase captures the defining physical characteristic of wave motion, including sound: a wave carries energy and momentum through a medium while the medium's particles only oscillate about fixed equilibrium positions and are not permanently displaced.
Any complex periodic signal can be written as a sum of sinusoids.

The resonance that occurs when air in a cavity vibrates like a mass on a spring: air in a narrow neck or opening acts as the mass, while the springiness of the enclosed air volume provides the restoring force, producing a single strong low-frequency resonance.
At its natural resonance a system responds with maximum amplitude to an applied force, and it is where energy is most efficiently stored and radiated.
The degree to which two or more sound waves or signals hold a stable phase relationship over time.
Acoustic energy density is the acoustic energy stored per unit volume of the medium, comprising kinetic energy of particle motion and potential energy of compression.
Acoustic energy flux is the rate at which acoustic energy passes through a surface, obtained by integrating sound intensity over that surface.
An acoustic field is the region of a medium in which sound waves are present, fully described at each point by sound pressure and particle velocity as functions of position and time.
An acoustic impedance mismatch is a difference in characteristic (specific) acoustic impedance between two media or regions, which causes partial reflection of a sound wave at their boundary.
Acoustic intensity is the time-averaged rate of acoustic energy flow per unit area in the direction of propagation, equal to the time average of the product of sound pressure and particle velocity.
Acoustic momentum is the linear momentum transported by a sound wave, whose time-averaged density for a plane travelling wave equals the acoustic energy density divided by the sound speed.
Acoustic power density is the acoustic power carried per unit area of a wavefront, numerically equal to the magnitude of the sound intensity and expressed in watts per square metre.
Acoustic resistance is the real, in-phase part of acoustic impedance, equal to the component of sound pressure that is in phase with the volume velocity divided by that volume velocity.

An acoustic singularity is a point in a sound field where a field quantity becomes infinite or undefined, such as the source point of an idealized point (monopole) source where the modelled pressure diverges, or a phase singularity (acoustic vortex) where amplitude vanishes and phase is undefined.

The acoustic velocity potential is a scalar function whose spatial gradient gives the particle velocity and whose time derivative (times minus the density) gives the sound pressure, valid for irrotational acoustic fields.
The acoustic wavelength is the spatial distance over which a sound wave completes one full cycle, equal to the sound speed divided by the frequency.
The acoustic wavenumber is the spatial rate of phase change of a sound wave, in acoustics conventionally the angular wavenumber k = 2*pi/lambda = omega/c, expressed in radians per metre.
The angular wavenumber is the number of radians of phase per unit length of a wave, defined as k = 2*pi/lambda and measured in radians per metre.
Bulk density is the mass of a material per unit of its total occupied volume, including any internal pores or air voids.

The characteristic (specific acoustic) impedance of a medium is the product of its density and sound speed, z0 = rho*c, equal to the ratio of acoustic pressure to particle velocity for a plane progressive wave.
A compression (longitudinal) wave is one in which particle motion is parallel to the direction of propagation, producing alternating regions of compression and rarefaction.
Distance-to-phase conversion expresses a propagation path length as an equivalent phase shift for a given frequency, phi = 2*pi*d/lambda = 2*pi*f*d/c.
An evanescent wave is a near-field disturbance whose amplitude decays exponentially with distance and which carries no net energy away from its source or interface.

Frequency-dependent directionality is the tendency of a source or receiver to radiate or pick up sound more selectively as frequency rises, because directivity depends on size relative to wavelength (ka).

The Helmholtz equation is the time-independent (frequency-domain) form of the wave equation, laplacian(p) + k^2*p = 0, obtained by assuming a time-harmonic pressure, where k = omega/c is the wavenumber.
The homogeneous acoustic wave equation is the source-free linear partial differential equation that governs small-amplitude sound pressure in a lossless, uniform fluid.
An impedance boundary condition specifies a surface by the ratio of acoustic pressure to normal particle velocity at that surface, rather than fixing pressure or velocity alone.
The inhomogeneous acoustic wave equation is the wave equation with a non-zero right-hand side representing acoustic sources within the region.
Instantaneous sound pressure is the momentary difference between the total pressure at a point and the ambient static pressure, at a given instant of time.
Kinetic energy density is the acoustic kinetic energy per unit volume in a sound field, arising from the motion of the fluid particles.
Linear acoustics is the branch of acoustics that treats sound as a small perturbation of the medium, so the governing equations are linearised and pressure disturbances add by superposition.
A natural frequency is a frequency at which a system tends to oscillate freely after an initial disturbance, in the absence of continuous forcing or damping.
Normal-incidence specific acoustic impedance is the complex ratio of sound pressure to normal particle velocity at a surface when a plane wave arrives perpendicularly.
Peak particle velocity is the maximum instantaneous speed of the medium's particles as they oscillate about their rest position in a sound field.
Acoustic potential energy density is the energy stored per unit volume in the compression of the medium by a sound field, equal to p^2/(2*rho*c^2) for the instantaneous pressure.

The propagation constant is a complex quantity, gamma = alpha + j*beta, describing how a harmonic wave changes as it travels: its real part alpha is the attenuation constant (amplitude decay per unit length) and its imaginary part beta is the phase constant (phase change per unit length, equal to the wavenumber k = omega/c in a lossless medium).
The radiation (Sommerfeld) boundary condition is the physical requirement that, far from a source, acoustic energy only travels outward and no waves arrive from infinity.
The reference sound pressure is the standardized pressure against which sound pressure level is defined: 20 micropascals (2e-5 Pa) in air and 1 micropascal in water.
